dialogue.title: Learning Professional Email Etiquette
dialogue.context: Ahmed's supervisor helps him revise a professional email that was too casual.

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Ahmed, I saw the email you sent to the client. The content is good, but the tone is too informal for a business communication.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: Really? I thought it was friendly. What's wrong with it?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: You started with 'Hey!' That's too casual for a first-time client. Use 'Dear Mr. Johnson' or 'Dear John' if you have an established relationship.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: I see. What about ending with 'Thanks!' - is that wrong too?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: For a casual colleague, it's fine. But for clients or senior management, use 'Thank you for your time and consideration' or 'I look forward to hearing from you.'

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: What about the subject line? I wrote 'Question.'

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Too vague. Be specific: 'Question Regarding Project Timeline' or 'Follow-up on Budget Discussion.' People get hundreds of emails - specific subjects help.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: And I wrote 'Can you send me that thing we talked about?' Should that be more formal?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Definitely. Try 'I would appreciate it if you could send the revised proposal we discussed in yesterday's meeting.' Be specific and polite.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: This is more complex than I thought. Is there a basic structure I should follow?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Yes: greeting, brief opening (state purpose), body (details), closing (action items), and professional sign-off. Let me show you an example.

lines.speaker: Ahmed
lines.text: That helps! So tone matches the relationship and situation?

lines.speaker: Supervisor
lines.text: Exactly. Formal for new contacts and sensitive topics, more casual for close colleagues on routine matters. When in doubt, err on the side of formality.

pattern_drills.pattern: I hope this email finds you well. I'm writing to...
examples: I hope this email finds you well. I'm writing to follow up on our meeting yesterday.
I hope you're doing well. I'm writing to request information about the project timeline.
I trust this email finds you well. I'm writing to confirm our appointment for next Tuesday.
I hope this message finds you well. I'm writing to discuss the budget proposal.
I hope you're having a good week. I'm writing to introduce our new team member.

pattern_drills.pattern: I would appreciate it if you could...
examples: I would appreciate it if you could send the report by Friday.
I would be grateful if you could review the attached document.
It would be helpful if you could provide your feedback by end of day.
I would appreciate your input on this matter at your earliest convenience.
Could you please confirm receipt of this email when you have a moment?

pattern_drills.pattern: Thank you for... / I look forward to...
examples: Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to hearing from you.
Thank you for your prompt attention to this matter.
I appreciate your assistance with this. Please let me know if you need any clarification.
Thank you in advance for your help. I look forward to your response.
I appreciate your understanding. Please don't hesitate to contact me if you have questions.

listening_exercises.transcript: Professional email structure has five parts: 1) Clear subject line that summarizes content. 2) Formal greeting (Dear...). 3) Opening stating purpose. 4) Body with details in short paragraphs. 5) Professional closing and signature. Keep emails concise - busy professionals appreciate brevity. If an email is longer than three paragraphs, consider a phone call instead.
listening_exercises.question: How many parts does professional email structure have?

listening_exercises.transcript: Email tone should match your relationship with the recipient and the situation's formality. For new contacts, supervisors, or sensitive topics, use formal language. For colleagues you know well on routine matters, you can be slightly more casual. Avoid slang, emoji, or excessive exclamation points in professional emails. When uncertain, choose formal over casual - you can always relax tone later.
listening_exercises.question: When should you use formal email tone?
options: For new contacts, supervisors, or sensitive topics

listening_exercises.transcript: Common email mistakes: vague subject lines, no greeting, unclear purpose, walls of text, demanding tone, and forgetting attachments. Always proofread before sending. For important emails, write a draft, wait an hour, then review with fresh eyes. Never send angry emails immediately - save as a draft and revisit when calm. Remember: emails are permanent records.
listening_exercises.question: What should you do before sending important emails?
options: Write a draft, wait, then review

speaking_tasks.prompt: You need to ask your supervisor for time off. Explain what you would say in a professional email (don't write it - speak it). Record for 25 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: If I were writing a professional email to request time off, I would start with a formal greeting like 'Dear Ms. Johnson.' Then I'd state my purpose clearly: 'I'm writing to request vacation time from June 15th to June 22nd.' I'd explain the reason briefly if appropriate: 'I'm planning to visit family who I haven't seen in two years.' Then I'd show consideration: 'I've reviewed the team calendar and confirmed this wouldn't conflict with major deadlines. I'll ensure all my current projects are completed before I leave.' Finally, I'd close professionally: 'Thank you for considering my request. Please let me know if you need any additional information.' This structure is clear, respectful, and professional.

speaking_tasks.prompt: Explain the difference between an email to a close colleague and one to a new client. Give examples. Record for 25 seconds.
speaking_tasks.example: The tone and formality differ significantly between colleagues and new clients. To a close colleague about a routine matter, I might write: 'Hi Sarah, can you send me that report when you get a chance? Thanks!' That's casual and brief. But to a new client, I'd write: 'Dear Mr. Anderson, I hope this email finds you well. I'm writing to request the quarterly report we discussed in our meeting on Monday. I would appreciate it if you could send it at your earliest convenience. Thank you for your time and consideration.' The second version is more formal, specific, and polite. As relationships develop, you can gradually become less formal, but always maintain professionalism.

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a professional email to a potential employer thanking them for an interview and expressing continued interest. Include: subject line, greeting, body, and closing. (100-120 words)
writing_tasks.example:
Subject: Thank You - Interview for Marketing Coordinator Position

Dear Ms. Thompson,

I hope this email finds you well. I'm writing to thank you for taking the time to interview me yesterday for the Marketing Coordinator position. I truly enjoyed our conversation about the company's digital strategy initiatives.

Our discussion reinforced my strong interest in joining your team. I was particularly excited to learn about the upcoming product launch campaign. My experience managing social media campaigns for previous employers aligns well with the responsibilities we discussed.

I appreciate the opportunity to learn more about the role and your vision for the marketing department. Please don't hesitate to contact me if you need any additional information.

Thank you again for your time and consideration. I look forward to hearing from you.

Best regards,
Ahmed Hassan

writing_tasks.prompt: Write a professional email to a client apologizing for a delayed response and providing the requested information. (80-100 words)
writing_tasks.example:
Subject: Response to Your Inquiry - Project Timeline

Dear Mr. Rodriguez,

I apologize for the delayed response to your inquiry from last week. We experienced unexpected system issues that affected our email access.

Regarding your question about the project timeline, I'm pleased to confirm that we're on schedule for the March 15th delivery date. The design phase is complete, and we've begun development. I've attached a detailed timeline showing each milestone.

I would appreciate it if you could review the attachment and let me know if you have any questions or concerns.

Thank you for your patience and understanding.

Best regards,
Ahmed Hassan

grammar_focus.title: Modal Verbs for Politeness (would, could, may)
grammar_focus.explanation: Use modal verbs to make requests and suggestions more polite in professional emails.
examples: I would appreciate your feedback. (more polite than 'I want')
Could you please send the report? (politer than 'Send the report')
You may wish to consider this alternative. (softer than 'You should')
Would it be possible to reschedule? (politer than 'Can we reschedule?')

grammar_focus.title: Passive Voice for Diplomacy
grammar_focus.explanation: Use passive voice to soften criticism or avoid assigning blame.
examples: An error was made in the report. (vs. 'You made an error')
The deadline was missed. (vs. 'You missed the deadline')
It has been brought to my attention... (formal and diplomatic)
The document needs to be revised. (softer than 'You need to revise')

grammar_focus.title: Conditional Statements for Suggestions
grammar_focus.explanation: Use conditionals to make suggestions less direct and more diplomatic.
examples: It would be helpful if you could attend. (suggestion)
If you have time, please review the attachment. (polite request)
It might be beneficial to consider alternatives. (gentle suggestion)
If possible, I would appreciate an early response. (polite request)

cultural_notes: American business emails tend to be direct and concise - get to the point quickly after a brief greeting.
Email is the primary business communication in U.S. workplaces - response within 24 hours is expected.
Americans value work-life balance - avoid sending work emails late at night or on weekends unless urgent.
'Reply all' should be used carefully - only when everyone needs the information.
Out-of-office automatic replies are standard when on vacation or unavailable.
Professional email addresses should be firstname.lastname@company - not nicknames or unprofessional handles.
